use: Plans, work or relationships working out; umaku ikanai means it isn't working.

example.ja: 大丈夫、きっとうまくいくよ。

examplePolite.romaji: Daijoubu desu, kitto umaku ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、きっとうまくいきますよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't worry, I'm sure it'll work out.

notes: Past is umaku itta (it went well).

use: Any failure, from a big project to burning dinner.

example.ja: 今日の料理、失敗しちゃった。

examplePolite.romaji: Kyou no ryouri wa shippai shite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の料理は失敗してしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I'm afraid I messed up dinner today.

notes: X ni shippai suru: fail at X. Also a noun: shippai da (it's a flop). Opposite: seikou.

use: Sounds big for small things; for an everyday 'it worked', umaku iku is more natural.

example.ja: サプライズ、成功したね！

examplePolite.ja: サプライズは成功しましたね！

notes: Also a noun: daiseikou (a huge success). Opposite: shippai.

use: Something being made is finished: a building, a dish, a project.

example.ja: 模型、やっと完成したよ！

examplePolite.ja: 模型がやっと完成しました！

notes: The thing is the subject: ie ga kansei shita (the house is finished).

use: Passing an exam, interview or entrance test: shiken ni goukaku suru.
notes: Failing is ochiru: shiken ni ochita. goukaku omedetou! means 'congrats on passing'.

use: Repeating something to get better: sport, music, speaking.

example.romaji: Shiai no mae ni motto renshuu shiyou.
example.ja: 試合の前にもっと練習しよう。
example.english: Let's practise more before the match.

examplePolite.romaji: Shiai no mae ni motto renshuu shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 試合の前にもっと練習しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's practise more before the match.

notes: Also a noun: renshuu ni iku (go to practice).

use: Usually X ni shuuchuu suru (focus on X), or shuuchuu dekinai (can't focus).

example.ja: ここ、うるさくて集中できない。
example.english: It's too noisy here to focus.

examplePolite.ja: ここはうるさくて集中できません。
examplePolite.english: It's too noisy here to focus.

use: Learning from a teacher or in lessons: piano o narau.

example.ja: 子供のころ、ピアノ習ってた。
example.english: I took piano lessons as a kid.

examplePolite.romaji: Kodomo no koro, piano o naratte imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 子供のころ、ピアノを習っていました。
examplePolite.english: I took piano lessons as a child.

notes: For studying on your own, say benkyou suru.

use: Learning in a broad or serious sense, from experience, history or mistakes.

example.romaji: Kono shigoto de iroiro mananda yo.
example.ja: この仕事でいろいろ学んだよ。
example.english: I learned a lot from this job.

examplePolite.ja: この仕事でいろいろ学びました。
examplePolite.english: I learned a lot from this job.

notes: narau needs a teacher; manabu doesn't.

use: Working out numbers: a bill, costs, time.

example.ja: 一人いくらか計算して。
example.english: Work out how much it is each.

examplePolite.romaji: Hitori ikura ka keisan shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 一人いくらか計算してください。
examplePolite.english: Please work out how much it is per person.

notes: keisan doori: exactly as planned. keisan ga hayai: quick with numbers.

use: Being alive or living a certain way; not for where you live.

example.ja: 自分のために生きたい。
example.english: I want to live for myself.

examplePolite.romaji: Jibun no tame ni ikitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 自分のために生きたいです。
examplePolite.english: I want to live for myself.

notes: Where you live is sumu: Tokyo ni sunde iru. ikiteru means 'alive'.

use: Day-to-day living, who with and how: hitori de kurasu (live alone).

example.ja: 今は一人で暮らしてる。
example.english: I live on my own now.

examplePolite.romaji: Ima wa hitori de kurashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は一人で暮らしています。
examplePolite.english: I live on my own now.

notes: Noun: kurashi (life, lifestyle); hitorigurashi is living alone.

use: Spending a stretch of time a certain way: holidays, weekends, time with someone.

example.english: How did you spend the weekend?

examplePolite.ja: 週末はどう過ごしましたか？
examplePolite.english: How did you spend the weekend?

use: The mother is the subject: kodomo o umu (have a child).

example.romaji: Ane ga onna no ko o unda n da.
example.ja: 姉が女の子を産んだんだ。
example.english: My sister had a baby girl.

examplePolite.romaji: Ane ga onna no ko o umimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 姉が女の子を産みました。
examplePolite.english: My sister had a baby girl.

notes: 'Be born' is umareru: Tokyo de umareta (I was born in Tokyo).

use: Where or how someone grew up; also plants and animals growing.

example.romaji: Kono machi de sodatta n da.
example.english: I grew up in this town.

examplePolite.english: I grew up in this town.

notes: To raise a child is sodateru: kodomo o sodateru.

use: Growing up or developing: a child, a person who has matured, a company.

examplePolite.romaji: Kare wa sugoku seichou shimashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はすごく成長しましたね。

notes: More about growing as a person than sodatsu. Also a noun: seichou ga tanoshimi (can't wait to see you grow).

english: be late (for school, work, a meeting)
use: Late for a fixed start time.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと遅刻する。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、少し遅刻します。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I'll be a little late.

notes: okureru is the general 'be late': densha ga okureta (the train was late).

use: Skipping something you should do, or slacking off while you're there.

example.ja: 昨日、仕事サボっちゃったんだ。

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は仕事をサボりました。

use: Saying where you're employed: X ni tsutomete iru.

example.english: My brother works at a bank.

examplePolite.romaji: Ani wa ginkou ni tsutomete imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 兄は銀行に勤めています。
examplePolite.english: My brother works at a bank.

notes: hataraku is 'work' in general; tsutomeru is being on a company's staff.
